<role>
# Your role: the company's press officer

You are the press officer for one company, in a public demo of flatbed. The visitor gave you the company's web address in their first message. You have never worked there and know nothing about it beyond what its public pages say, so everything you write rests on those pages. The company has not asked for any of this and approves none of it, which is why every draft you write is marked as an unofficial demo draft.

Your work has three parts, in this order: read the company's pages, write down what you learned, then draft what the visitor asks for. A careful press officer works this way because a draft is only as good as the facts under it, and a fact you cannot point to is one a journalist will ask about.

## Read a handful of pages

`fetch_page` reads one public page and saves its text into `sources/`, with the links it found. Each page costs time and money in this demo, so aim for about six pages per company, and stop sooner if you have what you need. These have given the most for the fewest pages:

- the home page, which says what the company does and for whom, in its own words
- the about page, for when it started, where it is, who runs it and why
- one or two product or pricing pages, for what it sells
- the blog or news page, and perhaps one recent post, for what it has said lately and how it writes

Pick the next page from the links the last one returned, rather than guessing addresses. When a page cannot be fetched, the tool says why; try the next most useful link rather than the same one again.

## Write the fact sheet

Write `notes/fact-sheet` once you have read the pages. It is your memory of the company. Pin it with `pin_doc`, so you see it in every later session. Write each fact as a short line with the page behind it, such as:

```
- Makes scheduling software for dental clinics (sources/quillfern-example-home)
- Founded in 2019 in Leeds (sources/quillfern-example-about)
- Named people: Ada Quill, co-founder and CEO (sources/quillfern-example-about)
```

Copy numbers, names and dates exactly as the page gives them, because the supervisor checks drafts against the page and not against your notes. List the people the site names, with their roles, since they are the only people a draft can quote. When the pages leave something out, such as how many customers the company has, write that it is not stated. That gap is useful: it tells you what a draft cannot say.

## Write the voice guide

Write `notes/voice-guide` from how the company writes, and pin it too. A few lines are enough: how formal it is, how long its sentences are, whether it says "we" or its own name, words it uses often and words it avoids, and one short phrase quoted from a page to show the register. The supervisor reads it when it checks a draft's tone, so describe what you saw, not what you would like.

## Draft

Write each draft into `outbox/`, with a name that says what it is, such as `outbox/launch-announcement`. Before you draft, read the pages behind the facts you plan to use with `read_doc`, unless you fetched them in this session. The supervisor sees only what is in this session, and a true claim from a page it cannot see will be refused.

What the supervisor checks, and so what works:

- Every claim about the company is on a page in `sources/`. When the visitor asks for something the pages do not support, such as a customer count, leave it out and say so in your reply, or write a placeholder in square brackets, such as `[number of customers, to be confirmed]`.
- No invented numbers, customers, partners, awards or prices. Round numbers you made up to sound confident are the most common slip.
- Quotes use only words a page gives, attributed to the person the page names. Otherwise write a placeholder: `[Quote from Ada Quill, CEO, to be supplied]`, or `[Quote from a company spokesperson]` when the site names nobody. Putting new words in a real person's mouth is the one thing a press office must never do without their approval.
- No promises about the future, such as dates, features or prices to come, unless a page states them; then say the company has said so.
- The tone follows the voice guide.
- The draft ends with this line, in italics: `_Unofficial draft written by an AI agent in the flatbed playground demo. Not from or approved by <company name>._`

When a draft is refused, read what the supervisor found, fix those lines, and write it again. Tell the visitor briefly what was refused and why: seeing a claim caught is part of what the demo shows. If you cannot fix it from the pages you have, say what is missing rather than writing around it.

A reply to a journalist about something the pages do not cover, such as a rumour, works best as a polite reply that says only what the pages support and does not confirm or deny the rest.
</role>

<documents>
You keep a set of Markdown documents, and they are your memory. Each session starts with no memory of the last one: you know what is pinned below and what you can read with read_doc. Before a session ends, write down what the next one will need, because anything not written down is lost.

Pin a document when you need it in every session, such as who you are and how you work. Pinned documents follow this section. Leave the rest unpinned and find them with list_docs. A change to a document, or to what is pinned, reaches your context at the next session.

Give every document a one-line summary that says what it is for, and a name like a path, such as people/tomas-reyes. Keep a document as the current state of its subject: rewrite a line when it stops being true rather than adding another.

Your timeline has one document a day, named timeline/YYYY-MM-DD. You see today's in full and one summary line for each of the six days before it. When something happens that a later session would want to know, add a line with add_to_timeline, and keep the day's summary true.
</documents>

<folders>
Your documents are kept in folders, and each folder's mode says what you can do there. You can read and write a document outside these folders freely.

- read: you can list and read these documents, but not change them.
- write: you can read and write these freely.
- reviewed: you can read these. A supervisor checks each write before it lands, and a write that fails comes back to you with what failed, so you can redraft and write again.

<folder path="sources/" mode="read">The company's public pages, one document each, saved by fetch_page. The only evidence a draft can rest on.</folder>
<folder path="notes/" mode="write">Your working notes: the fact sheet, with the page behind each fact, and the voice guide.</folder>
<folder path="outbox/" mode="reviewed">Drafts for publication. A supervisor checks each one against the pages in sources/ before it lands.</folder>
</folders>

tools.name: list_docs
tools.description: List your documents, one line each with its summary. Use it to find a document before you read or write it, and before you start a new one, so you add to an existing document rather than making a second.

prefix.description: Only names starting with this, such as people/

tools.name: read_doc
tools.description: Read one of your documents in full. Read a document before you change it, unless it is pinned and already in your context.

tools.name: write_doc
tools.description: Write a whole document, creating it or replacing its body, for a new document or a rewrite. To change one passage, use edit_doc instead. The previous version is kept.

summary.description: One line saying what the document is for. Required for a new document; leave it out to keep the current one.

tools.name: edit_doc
tools.description: Change one passage of a document by replacing it exactly. Copy the passage from the document as it is now, with enough around it to occur only once. Use an empty replacement to delete it.

tools.name: pin_doc
tools.description: Pin a document so it is in your context at the start of every session, or unpin it. Pin what you need every time; every pinned document costs room in every session.

pinned.description: true to pin, false to unpin

tools.name: add_to_timeline
tools.description: Add a line to today's timeline. Use it whenever something happens that a later session would want to know: what was asked, decided, sent or promised. Later sessions see only the day's summary, so keep it true as the day goes on.

line.description: One line, such as "Tomas Reyes asked to move Thursday's call to Friday."

summary.description: One line for the whole day so far. Give it when the day has changed its shape; leave it out to keep the current one.

tools.name: fetch_page
tools.description: Read one public web page and save its text in sources/. Returns the saved text and the links on the page. Aim for about six pages per company: the home page, about, a product page and the blog or news page.

url.description: The full address, such as https://example.com/about

tools.name: reset
tools.description: End this session and start a fresh one. Call it when your notes are up to date and the session is long, or when the work is finished. Anything not written down will be forgotten.

Plausible Analytics is an independent, open source analytics company based in the EU. We built it because web analytics had drifted far from its purpose: a simple way for site owners to understand their traffic without surveilling their visitors.

We do not use cookies and we do not collect personal data. No surveillance model, no data brokerage, no conflict of interest between what we sell and what our customers need.

More than 21,000 paying subscribers use Plausible. Stripe, Mozilla, Basecamp, Ghost, Hugging Face, Home Assistant, MongoDB, the Python Software Foundation and Harvard University are among the names running it.

## Our story

Uku Taht started Plausible in December 2018, building it alone as a simple privacy-friendly alternative to Google Analytics. Paid subscriptions launched in 2019.

In 2020, when it was still just Uku building and a few hundred paying customers, Marko Saric joined to handle marketing and communications. No outside funding, no growth team. The company has grown through product improvement and transparent communication ever since.

Plausible crossed $1 million in annual recurring revenue in 2022 and has continued to grow as a profitable, independently operated company.

You can read a detailed account of our early decisions and growth in our startup journey article .

Today Plausible is a team of 10. You can meet everyone on our team page .

## How we’re funded

We are self-funded and profitable, with no outside investors and no plans to sell. Subscription revenue is the only revenue we have. It funds our team, infrastructure and product development. We do not sell or share customer data and we do not monetize visitor behavior.

Our primary obligation is to our customers. They fund the company and guide its direction, because no one else does.

## How we grow

We have never spent a cent on advertising, affiliates or paid endorsements. Plausible grows because people recommend it when they have no reason to other than that it works. That kind of trust cannot be bought, and it says more about the product than anything we could claim about ourselves.

## Open source as accountability

Plausible is open source under the GNU Affero General Public License Version 3 (AGPLv3).

Our source code is publicly available and can be inspected, reviewed and verified at any time. Open source, combined with a sustainable commercial model, ensures transparency and long-term maintenance.

Customers are not locked in. If we were ever to make decisions that went against our stated values, the code can be forked and developed independently.

## Privacy without compromise

We built Plausible to prove that useful web analytics and visitor privacy are not mutually exclusive.

We do not use cookies and we do not collect personal data. We do not perform cross-site or cross-device tracking. For full details, see our Data Policy and Security documentation .

Plausible is not the right tool for every analytics use case. Read when Plausible is not a fit before you decide.

## What GA4 changed and why it matters

### GA4 replaced real data with estimated data

This is the most consequential change and the least discussed one.

GA4 introduced “consent mode”: a system that, when a visitor declines cookie consent, fills the gap with behavioral modeling. GA4 estimates what that visitor probably did based on similar users who did consent. You are no longer looking at what happened on your site. You are looking at a blend of what happened and what Google’s model thinks happened.

On sites with high opt-out rates, that modeling can represent a large share of reported traffic. There is no way to distinguish modeled data from real data in standard GA4 reports.

Plausible collects no personal data and requires no consent banner. Every visit in your dashboard is a real visit.

### GA4 became significantly harder to use

Universal Analytics had flaws, but you could get to the numbers you needed. GA4 rebuilt the interface around Google’s event-based data model: a model designed for app telemetry and then applied to websites.

The result: basic tasks that took one click in Universal Analytics now require setting up custom events in Tag Manager, navigating “Explorations” (a separate reporting surface from the main dashboard), or writing SQL queries against a BigQuery export. Google provides no real support when something isn’t working.

Plausible gives you all the important metrics on one page: visitors, sources, pages, countries, devices, goals and revenue attribution. You can invite team members, connect to Search Console, build custom reports in Data Studio, import your historical data and use features like funnels, user journeys and realtime reporting. See what it looks like on our live demo .

### GA4 made accuracy worse, not better

GA4 misses a substantial share of traffic compared to what actually visits your site.

The consent banner alone accounts for most of it. An independent study found that GA4 fails to capture an average of 55.6% of traffic compared to cookieless analytics. Use our cookie banner traffic loss calculator to estimate the gap on your own site.

Beyond consent, GA4 is part of the adtech ecosystem. Most adblockers target it specifically. With tech-savvy audiences, the share of people blocking Google Analytics can reach 60%.

Plausible doesn’t require consent and isn’t part of the adtech ecosystem, so it’s far less likely to be blocked . You can also proxy our script through your own domain for first-party collection. Additional accuracy improvements built in by default:

- Known referrer spam and data center traffic is filtered out. We exclude around 40,800 data center IP ranges to prevent bot inflation that GA4 doesn’t handle automatically.

- Android app traffic is properly attributed. GA4 traditionally lumps this into “Direct / None.” For sites with significant mobile traffic, this accounts for 10% or more of previously unattributed visits from apps like Gmail, Slack and Telegram.

- VPN and Tor traffic is grouped under “Anonymous VPN Service” to reduce location noise.

We also tested this directly. See how Plausible handled bot traffic in a head-to-head test with GA4. Here are more reasons Plausible is more accurate than GA4.

### GA4 created legal exposure

Since January 2022, data protection authorities in Austria, France, Italy, Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden have ruled that using Google Analytics violates GDPR . The rulings relate to EEA-US data transfers under Schrems II.

GA4’s current legality in Europe rests on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. That framework is in trouble. In June 2026, the US Supreme Court ended the independence of the FTC , the agency the EU relies on to enforce the framework, and Max Schrems and noyb responded by asking the European Commission to withdraw it while preparing a challenge at the EU’s top court. A separate case against it is already pending there. The two previous EU-US transfer deals were both struck down in court.

Staying compliant with GA4 requires cookie consent banners, a detailed privacy policy covering analytics tracking and in many cases a paid consent management platform. Each of those adds cost and friction. And if the framework falls, the legal basis for sending visitor data to Google’s US servers falls with it.

Plausible processes all visitor data on servers owned and operated by European providers. Your data never leaves the EU. Because Plausible doesn’t use cookies or collect personal data, you don’t need an analytics cookie consent banner under most privacy regulations.

An independent legal assessment comparing Plausible and Google Analytics written by a data protection lawyer is available if you want the detail.

### GA4 is built for Google’s business, not yours

Google Analytics is free because collecting behavioral data from millions of websites serves Google’s advertising operation. Your visitors’ data flows back to Google and becomes part of the system that powers ad targeting.

GA4 was specifically designed to make that data collection work in a world with more privacy restrictions. For Google’s benefit, not yours. Consent mode exists to keep the data flowing even when users opt out.

Universal Analytics was shut down when it stopped serving that purpose, with no real migration path and years of historical data deleted. GA4 will be no different when Google’s priorities shift again.

Plausible doesn’t participate in that model. No personal data is collected or shared. Nothing is sold to third parties. We don’t track visitors across sites. Your data stays in your account, in the EU, and is not used for anything other than showing you your own stats.

Plausible is open source. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub and anyone can audit exactly how data is handled, something Google Analytics has never allowed.

## Faster and lighter

Every script you add to a page has a performance cost. The Google Analytics tracking script is 135KB gzipped. Plausible’s is 2.5KB, which is 54 times smaller.

This matters for your visitors and for search rankings. See how the difference compounds with our analytics script size calculator , or read more about what makes Plausible a lightweight analytics tool .

## What GA4 does better

If you need deep custom attribution modeling or enterprise-scale reporting with SQL access, GA4, especially with BigQuery, has more depth. If your business runs heavily on Google Ads, the tight integration between GA4 and Google’s ad products is hard to replicate elsewhere.

For most site owners who want to understand where their traffic is coming from and what’s working, that depth comes with overhead that is rarely justified.

## Why isn’t Plausible free while GA4 is free?

GA4 is free because Google’s business runs on data. Collecting analytics from millions of websites is part of how they build the behavioral profiles that power their ad network.

Plausible doesn’t use that model. We charge a subscription to cover costs and keep the product independent.

If you’re using GA4 and wondering whether it’s still the right tool, that’s a reasonable question. Here’s a direct comparison.

## What GA4 changed and why it matters

### GA4 replaced real data with estimated data

This is the most consequential change and the least discussed one.

GA4 introduced “consent mode”: a system that, when a visitor declines cookie consent, fills the gap with behavioral modeling. GA4 estimates what that visitor probably did based on similar users who did consent. You are no longer looking at what happened on your site. You are looking at a blend of what happened and what Google’s model thinks happened.

On sites with high opt-out rates, that modeling can represent a large share of reported traffic. There is no way to distinguish modeled data from real data in standard GA4 reports.

Plausible collects no personal data and requires no consent banner. Every visit in your dashboard is a real visit.

### GA4 became significantly harder to use

Universal Analytics had flaws, but you could get to the numbers you needed. GA4 rebuilt the interface around Google’s event-based data model: a model designed for app telemetry and then applied to websites.

The result: basic tasks that took one click in Universal Analytics now require setting up custom events in Tag Manager, navigating “Explorations” (a separate reporting surface from the main dashboard), or writing SQL queries against a BigQuery export. Google provides no real support when something isn’t working.

Plausible gives you all the important metrics on one page: visitors, sources, pages, countries, devices, goals and revenue attribution. You can invite team members, connect to Search Console, build custom reports in Data Studio, import your historical data and use features like funnels, user journeys and realtime reporting. See what it looks like on our live demo .

### GA4 made accuracy worse, not better

GA4 misses a substantial share of traffic compared to what actually visits your site.

The consent banner alone accounts for most of it. An independent study found that GA4 fails to capture an average of 55.6% of traffic compared to cookieless analytics. Use our cookie banner traffic loss calculator to estimate the gap on your own site.

Beyond consent, GA4 is part of the adtech ecosystem. Most adblockers target it specifically. With tech-savvy audiences, the share of people blocking Google Analytics can reach 60%.

Plausible doesn’t require consent and isn’t part of the adtech ecosystem, so it’s far less likely to be blocked . You can also proxy our script through your own domain for first-party collection. Additional accuracy improvements built in by default:

- Known referrer spam and data center traffic is filtered out. We exclude around 40,800 data center IP ranges to prevent bot inflation that GA4 doesn’t handle automatically.

- Android app traffic is properly attributed. GA4 traditionally lumps this into “Direct / None.” For sites with significant mobile traffic, this accounts for 10% or more of previously unattributed visits from apps like Gmail, Slack and Telegram.

- VPN and Tor traffic is grouped under “Anonymous VPN Service” to reduce location noise.

We also tested this directly. See how Plausible handled bot traffic in a head-to-head test with GA4. Here are more reasons Plausible is more accurate than GA4.

### GA4 created legal exposure

Since January 2022, data protection authorities in Austria, France, Italy, Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden have ruled that using Google Analytics violates GDPR . The rulings relate to EEA-US data transfers under Schrems II.

GA4’s current legality in Europe rests on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. That framework is in trouble. In June 2026, the US Supreme Court ended the independence of the FTC , the agency the EU relies on to enforce the framework, and Max Schrems and noyb responded by asking the European Commission to withdraw it while preparing a challenge at the EU’s top court. A separate case against it is already pending there. The two previous EU-US transfer deals were both struck down in court.

Staying compliant with GA4 requires cookie consent banners, a detailed privacy policy covering analytics tracking and in many cases a paid consent management platform. Each of those adds cost and friction. And if the framework falls, the legal basis for sending visitor data to Google’s US servers falls with it.

Plausible processes all visitor data on servers owned and operated by European providers. Your data never leaves the EU. Because Plausible doesn’t use cookies or collect personal data, you don’t need an analytics cookie consent banner under most privacy regulations.

An independent legal assessment comparing Plausible and Google Analytics written by a data protection lawyer is available if you want the detail.

### GA4 is built for Google’s business, not yours

Google Analytics is free because collecting behavioral data from millions of websites serves Google’s advertising operation. Your visitors’ data flows back to Google and becomes part of the system that powers ad targeting.

GA4 was specifically designed to make that data collection work in a world with more privacy restrictions. For Google’s benefit, not yours. Consent mode exists to keep the data flowing even when users opt out.

Universal Analytics was shut down when it stopped serving that purpose, with no real migration path and years of historical data deleted. GA4 will be no different when Google’s priorities shift again.

Plausible doesn’t participate in that model. No personal data is collected or shared. Nothing is sold to third parties. We don’t track visitors across sites. Your data stays in your account, in the EU, and is not used for anything other than showing you your own stats.

Plausible is open source. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub and anyone can audit exactly how data is handled, something Google Analytics has never allowed.

## Faster and lighter

Every script you add to a page has a performance cost. The Google Analytics tracking script is 135KB gzipped. Plausible’s is 2.5KB, which is 54 times smaller.

This matters for your visitors and for search rankings. See how the difference compounds with our analytics script size calculator , or read more about what makes Plausible a lightweight analytics tool .

## What GA4 does better

If you need deep custom attribution modeling or enterprise-scale reporting with SQL access, GA4, especially with BigQuery, has more depth. If your business runs heavily on Google Ads, the tight integration between GA4 and Google’s ad products is hard to replicate elsewhere.

For most site owners who want to understand where their traffic is coming from and what’s working, that depth comes with overhead that is rarely justified.

## Why isn’t Plausible free while GA4 is free?

GA4 is free because Google’s business runs on data. Collecting analytics from millions of websites is part of how they build the behavioral profiles that power their ad network.

Plausible doesn’t use that model. We charge a subscription to cover costs and keep the product independent.

“Free” is also relative. GA4 comes with hidden costs : time spent learning a complex interface, consent management platforms, legal exposure in GDPR-regulated markets and developer time maintaining a compliant setup. When you factor those in, Plausible often costs less in practice. See our pricing page .

## Is Plausible right for you?

Plausible is not the right fit for every use case. If you need session replay, user-level product analytics, retargeting or free hosted analytics, read this before you decide .

## Tone and formality

- Conversational yet professional, avoiding buzzwords
- Direct and honest; willing to acknowledge limits and criticism of competitors
- Thoughtful and deliberate; willing to explain the reasoning behind choices
- Claims are supported with evidence (stats, comparisons, testing)

## Sentence length and structure

- Mix of short, punchy statements and longer explanatory ones
- Bullet points used extensively for feature lists
- Short opening statements often precede longer explanations
- Example: "Google Analytics is overkill for most site owners. Plausible gives you clear, useful insights without complexity, training or prior analytics experience."

## First-person perspective

- Uses "we" frequently when speaking about company decisions and values
- Direct address to reader: "your site," "you need," "your customers"
- Acknowledges audience directly in communication

## Word choices and themes

- Favors "simple," "lightweight," "privacy-friendly," "independent," "transparent" as core descriptors
- Contrasts Plausible against surveillance capitalism and data brokerage
- Emphasizes freedom and lack of lock-in
- Uses "boring" positively when describing business practices ("The boring way to build a startup")
- Avoids hype; prefers measured language about growth

## Writing about competitors

- Critical but fair; acknowledges what GA4 does well
- Specific with examples and evidence
- Labels criticism with author attribution when it's opinion ("What GA4 Changed and Why It Matters" as fact, vs blog post titles that signal opinion)

## Specific phrases and language

- "No outside investors, no acquisition targets"
- "That kind of trust cannot be bought"
- "Useful web analytics and visitor privacy are not mutually exclusive"
- "Not locked in"
- "Surveillance capitalism"
- Quotes founders directly when discussing company philosophy

## Capitalization and formatting

- Uses emoji sparingly but intentionally (EU flag 🇪🇺, heart ❤️)
- Bolds key statistics and differentiators
- Uses section headers with personality ("People ❤️ Plausible," "It's time to ditch Google Analytics")

## Audience

- Addresses both technical and non-technical site owners
- Explains complex concepts (consent mode, behavioral modeling) in accessible language
- Assumes readers may be frustrated with GA4 or other tools, validates that feeling

Source: https://plausible.io/about
Fetched: 2026-10-19

Plausible Analytics is an independent, open source analytics company based in the EU. We built it because web analytics had drifted far from its purpose: a simple way for site owners to understand their traffic without surveilling their visitors.

We do not use cookies and we do not collect personal data. No surveillance model, no data brokerage, no conflict of interest between what we sell and what our customers need.

More than 21,000 paying subscribers use Plausible. Stripe, Mozilla, Basecamp, Ghost, Hugging Face, Home Assistant, MongoDB, the Python Software Foundation and Harvard University are among the names running it.

## Our story

Uku Taht started Plausible in December 2018, building it alone as a simple privacy-friendly alternative to Google Analytics. Paid subscriptions launched in 2019.

In 2020, when it was still just Uku building and a few hundred paying customers, Marko Saric joined to handle marketing and communications. No outside funding, no growth team. The company has grown through product improvement and transparent communication ever since.

Plausible crossed $1 million in annual recurring revenue in 2022 and has continued to grow as a profitable, independently operated company.

You can read a detailed account of our early decisions and growth in our startup journey article .

Today Plausible is a team of 10. You can meet everyone on our team page .

## How we’re funded

We are self-funded and profitable, with no outside investors and no plans to sell. Subscription revenue is the only revenue we have. It funds our team, infrastructure and product development. We do not sell or share customer data and we do not monetize visitor behavior.

Our primary obligation is to our customers. They fund the company and guide its direction, because no one else does.

## How we grow

We have never spent a cent on advertising, affiliates or paid endorsements. Plausible grows because people recommend it when they have no reason to other than that it works. That kind of trust cannot be bought, and it says more about the product than anything we could claim about ourselves.

## Open source as accountability

Plausible is open source under the GNU Affero General Public License Version 3 (AGPLv3).

Our source code is publicly available and can be inspected, reviewed and verified at any time. Open source, combined with a sustainable commercial model, ensures transparency and long-term maintenance.

Customers are not locked in. If we were ever to make decisions that went against our stated values, the code can be forked and developed independently.

## Privacy without compromise

We built Plausible to prove that useful web analytics and visitor privacy are not mutually exclusive.

We do not use cookies and we do not collect personal data. We do not perform cross-site or cross-device tracking. For full details, see our Data Policy and Security documentation .

Plausible is not the right tool for every analytics use case. Read when Plausible is not a fit before you decide.

Google didn’t upgrade Google Analytics in 2023. They replaced it. Universal Analytics was shut down, historical data was deleted, and everyone using Google Analytics was moved onto a product built from scratch around Google’s advertising infrastructure, not around the needs of website owners.

If you’re using GA4 and wondering whether it’s still the right tool, that’s a reasonable question. Here’s a direct comparison.

## What GA4 changed and why it matters

### GA4 replaced real data with estimated data

This is the most consequential change and the least discussed one.

GA4 introduced “consent mode”: a system that, when a visitor declines cookie consent, fills the gap with behavioral modeling. GA4 estimates what that visitor probably did based on similar users who did consent. You are no longer looking at what happened on your site. You are looking at a blend of what happened and what Google’s model thinks happened.

On sites with high opt-out rates, that modeling can represent a large share of reported traffic. There is no way to distinguish modeled data from real data in standard GA4 reports.

Plausible collects no personal data and requires no consent banner. Every visit in your dashboard is a real visit.

### GA4 became significantly harder to use

Universal Analytics had flaws, but you could get to the numbers you needed. GA4 rebuilt the interface around Google’s event-based data model: a model designed for app telemetry and then applied to websites.

The result: basic tasks that took one click in Universal Analytics now require setting up custom events in Tag Manager, navigating “Explorations” (a separate reporting surface from the main dashboard), or writing SQL queries against a BigQuery export. Google provides no real support when something isn’t working.

Plausible gives you all the important metrics on one page: visitors, sources, pages, countries, devices, goals and revenue attribution. You can invite team members, connect to Search Console, build custom reports in Data Studio, import your historical data and use features like funnels, user journeys and realtime reporting. See what it looks like on our live demo .

### GA4 made accuracy worse, not better

GA4 misses a substantial share of traffic compared to what actually visits your site.

The consent banner alone accounts for most of it. An independent study found that GA4 fails to capture an average of 55.6% of traffic compared to cookieless analytics. Use our cookie banner traffic loss calculator to estimate the gap on your own site.

Beyond consent, GA4 is part of the adtech ecosystem. Most adblockers target it specifically. With tech-savvy audiences, the share of people blocking Google Analytics can reach 60%.

Plausible doesn’t require consent and isn’t part of the adtech ecosystem, so it’s far less likely to be blocked . You can also proxy our script through your own domain for first-party collection. Additional accuracy improvements built in by default:

- Known referrer spam and data center traffic is filtered out. We exclude around 40,800 data center IP ranges to prevent bot inflation that GA4 doesn’t handle automatically.

- Android app traffic is properly attributed. GA4 traditionally lumps this into “Direct / None.” For sites with significant mobile traffic, this accounts for 10% or more of previously unattributed visits from apps like Gmail, Slack and Telegram.

- VPN and Tor traffic is grouped under “Anonymous VPN Service” to reduce location noise.

We also tested this directly. See how Plausible handled bot traffic in a head-to-head test with GA4. Here are more reasons Plausible is more accurate than GA4.

### GA4 created legal exposure

Since January 2022, data protection authorities in Austria, France, Italy, Denmark, Finland, Norway and Sweden have ruled that using Google Analytics violates GDPR . The rulings relate to EEA-US data transfers under Schrems II.

GA4’s current legality in Europe rests on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework. That framework is in trouble. In June 2026, the US Supreme Court ended the independence of the FTC , the agency the EU relies on to enforce the framework, and Max Schrems and noyb responded by asking the European Commission to withdraw it while preparing a challenge at the EU’s top court. A separate case against it is already pending there. The two previous EU-US transfer deals were both struck down in court.

Staying compliant with GA4 requires cookie consent banners, a detailed privacy policy covering analytics tracking and in many cases a paid consent management platform. Each of those adds cost and friction. And if the framework falls, the legal basis for sending visitor data to Google’s US servers falls with it.

Plausible processes all visitor data on servers owned and operated by European providers. Your data never leaves the EU. Because Plausible doesn’t use cookies or collect personal data, you don’t need an analytics cookie consent banner under most privacy regulations.

An independent legal assessment comparing Plausible and Google Analytics written by a data protection lawyer is available if you want the detail.

### GA4 is built for Google’s business, not yours

Google Analytics is free because collecting behavioral data from millions of websites serves Google’s advertising operation. Your visitors’ data flows back to Google and becomes part of the system that powers ad targeting.

GA4 was specifically designed to make that data collection work in a world with more privacy restrictions. For Google’s benefit, not yours. Consent mode exists to keep the data flowing even when users opt out.

Universal Analytics was shut down when it stopped serving that purpose, with no real migration path and years of historical data deleted. GA4 will be no different when Google’s priorities shift again.

Plausible doesn’t participate in that model. No personal data is collected or shared. Nothing is sold to third parties. We don’t track visitors across sites. Your data stays in your account, in the EU, and is not used for anything other than showing you your own stats.

Plausible is open source. Our source code is publicly available on GitHub and anyone can audit exactly how data is handled, something Google Analytics has never allowed.

## Faster and lighter

Every script you add to a page has a performance cost. The Google Analytics tracking script is 135KB gzipped. Plausible’s is 2.5KB, which is 54 times smaller.

This matters for your visitors and for search rankings. See how the difference compounds with our analytics script size calculator , or read more about what makes Plausible a lightweight analytics tool .

## What GA4 does better

If you need deep custom attribution modeling or enterprise-scale reporting with SQL access, GA4, especially with BigQuery, has more depth. If your business runs heavily on Google Ads, the tight integration between GA4 and Google’s ad products is hard to replicate elsewhere.

For most site owners who want to understand where their traffic is coming from and what’s working, that depth comes with overhead that is rarely justified.

## Why isn’t Plausible free while GA4 is free?

GA4 is free because Google’s business runs on data. Collecting analytics from millions of websites is part of how they build the behavioral profiles that power their ad network.

Plausible doesn’t use that model. We charge a subscription to cover costs and keep the product independent.

“Free” is also relative. GA4 comes with hidden costs : time spent learning a complex interface, consent management platforms, legal exposure in GDPR-regulated markets and developer time maintaining a compliant setup. When you factor those in, Plausible often costs less in practice. See our pricing page .

## Is Plausible right for you?

Plausible is not the right fit for every use case. If you need session replay, user-level product analytics, retargeting or free hosted analytics, read this before you decide .

## Ready to switch?

You can import your historical Google Analytics data so you don’t lose your historical stats. For a full walkthrough, see the GA to Plausible migration guide .
